Descriptive Combinatorics and Distributed AlgorithmsThanks: This is a draft of an article to appear in the October 2022 issue of the Notices of the AMS. This work is partially supported by the NSF grant DMS-2045412.

Anton Bernshteyn Address: School of Mathematics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA Email address: bahtoh@gatech.edu

In this article we shall explore a fascinating area called descriptive combinatorics and its recently discovered connections to distributed algorithms—a fundamental part of computer science that is becoming increasingly important in the modern era of decentralized computation. The interdisciplinary nature of these connections means that there is very little common background shared by the researchers who are interested in them. With this in mind, this article was written under the assumption that the reader would have close to no background in either descriptive set theory or computer science. The reader will judge to what degree this endeavor was successful.

The article comprises two parts. In the first part we give a brief introduction to some of the central notions and problems of descriptive combinatorics. The second part is devoted to a survey of some of the results concerning the interactions between descriptive combinatorics and distributed algorithms, as well as a few open problems.

1.  A brief introduction to descriptive combinatorics

1.1.  Basic notions of descriptive set theory

1.1.1.  Countable computation and Borel sets

Descriptive combinatorics is an area that emerged quite recently (about two decades ago) as the result of a symbiosis between combinatorics (especially graph theory) and descriptive set theory. For excellent surveys of this subject, see [KM20] by Kechris and Marks and [Pik21] by Pikhurko. In addition to combinatorics and descriptive set theory, descriptive combinatorics has close connections to numerous other branches of mathematics, such as ergodic theory, topological dynamics, probability theory, and model theory, to name a few.

To motivate the questions studied in descriptive combinatorics, it will be beneficial to first briefly discuss descriptive set theory more abstractly.

One way (out of many) of thinking about descriptive set theory is that it provides a versatile framework for gauging the inherent difficulty of mathematical problems pertaining to countable structures, in a manner analogous to how computational complexity theory gauges the inherent difficulty of finite problems. To pursue this analogy further, we can naturally present the basic concepts of descriptive set theory using a particular model of computation, namely Boolean circuits. An example of an (infinite) Boolean circuit is shown in Fig. 1. It is a network consisting of nodes, also called gates, joined by directed edges, or wires. The bottom layer comprises the input nodes. Each input node receives a bit value—00 or 11. The values then propagate through the network along the wires, with every gate computing a particular Boolean function of the values that feed into it: not, and, or or. Finally, one or more nodes are designated as the outputs. Thus, a Boolean circuit can be used to compute a function {0,1}In→{0,1}Out\{0,1\}^{\mathrm{In}}\to\{0,1\}^{\mathrm{Out}}, where In\mathrm{In} and Out\mathrm{Out} are the sets of the input and the output nodes respectively. For example, the circuit in Fig. 1 computes the function {0,1}ℕ→{0,1}\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\to\{0,1\} that equals 11 if and only if the input string does not contain two consecutive 11s.

There is one technical issue that we must make explicit here. Not every directed network can be used to perform well-defined computation. For instance, if a network involves a directed cycle of nodes, such as v0←v1←v2←⋯←v0v_{0}\leftarrow v_{1}\leftarrow v_{2}\leftarrow\cdots\leftarrow v_{0}, then the computational process wouldn’t even be able to start. More generally, a Boolean circuit must be well-founded, meaning that it must not contain an infinite descending sequence of nodes such as v0←v1←v2←v3←⋯v_{0}\leftarrow v_{1}\leftarrow v_{2}\leftarrow v_{3}\leftarrow\cdots. It is not hard to show that well-foundedness is the only necessary requirement: any well-founded network of gates implements a well-defined function.

An important part of computational complexity theory is circuit complexity, which studies how large a (finite) circuit needs to be to compute a given function f:{0,1}n→{0,1}mf\colon\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{m}. In descriptive set theory we are similarly interested in functions that can be computed by countable circuits:

Definition 1.1 (Borel subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}).

A subset A⊆{0,1}ℕA\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is Borel if its characteristic function can be computed by a countable Boolean circuit. We let 𝔅⁡({0,1}ℕ)\mathfrak{B}(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}) denote the family of all Borel subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}.

While Definition 1.1 applies to subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, it can naturally be extended to sets of other types, as long as their members can be somehow encoded by infinite bit strings. For example, a countable graph GG with vertex set V={v0,v1,v2,…}V=\{v_{0},v_{1},v_{2},\ldots\} can be represented by its adjacency matrix MGM_{G}, i.e., a countable table of 00s and 11s whose entry in row ii and column jj is 11 if and only if viv_{i} and vjv_{j} are adjacent in GG. We can then call a set AA of countable graphs Borel if there is a countable Boolean circuit that decides, given the matrix MGM_{G}, whether GG is in AA or not. For instance, the following sets of countable graphs are Borel:

{G:G is connected},{G:G is bipartite},{G:G is 3-colorable}.\displaystyle\{G\,:\,\text{$G$ is connected}\},\qquad\{G\,:\,\text{$G$ is bipartite}\},\qquad\{G\,:\,\text{$G$ is $3$-colorable}\}.

(The last one may be a bit surprising, since deciding whether a finite graph is 33-colorable is believed to be a computationally difficult problem. The difficulty miraculously disappears in the countable world, however.) On the other hand, the following set can be shown to not be Borel:

{G:G has an infinite clique}.\{G\,:\,\text{$G$ has an infinite clique}\}.

In fact, this set is complete analytic, which is a notion somewhat analogous to NP-completeness from computational complexity, with the added benefit that in descriptive set theory it is a theorem (due to Suslin from 1917; see [Kec95, §26]) that complete analytic sets cannot be Borel. In general, most subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} are not Borel: {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} has 22ℵ02^{2^{\aleph_{0}}} subsets but only 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}} of them are Borel (this result follows by enumerating all countable Boolean circuits).

1.1.2.  Borel sets in Polish spaces

A useful (and more classical) perspective on Borel sets is provided by topological considerations. We can define the distance between two infinite bit strings xx, y∈{0,1}ℕy\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} by the formula

dist⁡(x,y)≔∑n=0∞12n+1​|xn−yn|.\mathrm{dist}(x,y)\,\coloneqq\,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}|x_{n}-y_{n}|.

(This can be thought of as a weighted version of the Hamming distance.) The coefficients 1/2n+11/2^{n+1} are chosen so that the series ∑n=0∞1/2n+1\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}1/2^{n+1} converges (and hence the metric dist\mathrm{dist} is bounded, in this case by 11), but otherwise they are arbitrary. In particular, using a different convergent series with positive terms would yield a different metric, but the resulting topology on the space {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} would be the same—namely, it is the product topology arising from viewing {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} as the product of countably many copies of the discrete space {0,1}\{0,1\}. Actually, it is not hard to explicitly describe this topology without referring to the metric: a set A⊆{0,1}ℕA\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is open if and only if for every sequence x=(x0,x1,x2,…)∈Ax=(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots)\in A, the membership of xx in AA can be confirmed by looking at only finitely many entries of xx. More formally, AA is open if for each x∈Ax\in A, there is some n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} such that every infinite bit string whose first nn entries are (x0,x1,…,xn−1)(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}) is in AA.

Now, it turns out that Borel subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} can be described in purely topological terms and without any reference to Boolean circuits as follows: 𝔅⁡({0,1}ℕ)\mathfrak{B}(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}) is the smallest family of subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} that includes all open sets and is closed under countable Boolean operations (i.e., complements, countable unions, and countable intersections). And this characterization can be taken as the definition of Borel subsets of any topological space:

Definition 1.2 (Borel sets in topological spaces).

Let XX be a topological space. We let 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X) be the smallest family of subsets of XX that includes all open sets and is closed under countable Boolean operations. A subset A⊆XA\subseteq X is Borel if it is a member of 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X).

Although Definition 1.2 makes sense for an arbitrary topological space XX, descriptive set theory is mostly concerned with so-called Polish spaces. Formally, a topological space is Polish if it is second-countable (i.e., it has a countable basis) and completely metrizable (i.e., the topology is generated by a complete metric). A particularly compelling reason for focusing on Polish spaces is that the points of a Polish space can be encoded by infinite bit strings in a “well-behaved” way. This statement is made precise by the following remarkable theorem:

Theorem 1.3 (Borel Isomorphism Theorem [Kec95, Theorem 15.6]).

If XX is an uncountable Polish space, then there is a bijection 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐞:X→{0,1}ℕ\mathbf{code}\colon X\to\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} such that a set A⊆XA\subseteq X is Borel in XX if and only if the set {𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐞⁡(x):x∈A}\{\mathbf{code}(x)\,:\,x\in A\} is Borel in {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}.

In other words, the computational definition of Borel subsets of {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} given in Definition 1.1 can also be used to identify, via an appropriate coding, Borel sets in any uncountable Polish space. This is a powerful observation because many natural examples of topological spaces are Polish, for instance ℝ\mathbb{R} and, more generally, ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} for n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, the infinite-dimensional space ℝℕ\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}, the Baire space ℕℕ{\mathbb{N}}^{\mathbb{N}}, the unit intervals [0,1][0,1], (0,1)(0,1), and [0,1)[0,1), the unit circle 𝕊1\mathbb{S}^{1} and, more generally, any second-countable topological manifold, all compact metric spaces, all separable Banach spaces, etc. Furthermore, it is possible to parameterize various classes of mathematical structures by points in suitably defined Polish spaces. We have already seen how to use adjacency matrices to form a Polish space of countable graphs. In a similar vein, one can assemble, e.g., a Polish space of countable groups. There are also natural Polish spaces of continuous functions, measure-preserving transformations, separable Banach spaces, etc. It is even possible to define a Polish space of all Polish spaces!11 1 For the interested reader, we sketch the construction of the Polish space of Polish spaces. First, it turns out that every Polish space is homeomorphic to a closed subset of ℝℕ\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}. Now, let (Un)n∈ℕ(U_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be a countable basis for the topology of ℝℕ\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}. To each closed set X⊆ℝℕX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}, we assign a code 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐞X∈{0,1}ℕ\mathbf{code}_{X}\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} as follows: 𝐜𝐨𝐝𝐞X​(n)=1\mathbf{code}_{X}(n)=1 if and only if X∩Un≠∅X\cap U_{n}\neq\varnothing. Let 𝒳⊆{0,1}ℕ\mathcal{X}\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} be the set of all codes of closed subsets of ℝℕ\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}. One can show that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is Polish in the relative topology inherited from {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}. Thus, all Polish spaces are parameterized by the points of the Polish space 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

1.1.3.  Other classes of sets in descriptive set theory

In addition to Borel sets, there are various other classes of sets that play an important role in descriptive set theory. In this section we briefly introduce three such classes.

Let us temporarily return to the space {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} of infinite bit strings. Recall that a set A⊆{0,1}ℕA\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is Borel if the membership in AA can be decided by a countable Boolean circuit. Sometimes it makes sense to inquire whether a set is not just Borel but open. As mentioned in §1.1.2, a set A⊆{0,1}ℕA\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is open if for every sequence x∈Ax\in A, the membership of xx in AA can be confirmed by looking at only finitely many bits of xx. Of course, we can also investigate open sets in any other Polish space.

On the other hand, sometimes a set we are working with may not be Borel and yet be “almost” Borel in a certain suitable sense. For instance, a set A⊆{0,1}ℕA\subseteq\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is measurable if there is a countable Boolean circuit that correctly decides the membership in AA for a random input point x∈{0,1}ℕx\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}. More precisely, AA is measurable if there is a countable Boolean circuit CC with the following property. Let 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} denote the characteristic function of AA. Sample a sequence x=(x0,x1,x2,…)∈{0,1}ℕx=(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots)\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} randomly by making each xix_{i} be 00 or 11 independently with probability 1/21/2. Then C​(x)=𝟏A​(x)C(x)=\mathbf{1}_{A}(x) with probability 11; in other words, CC may fail to correctly determine xx’s membership in AA, but the probability of failure is 00. We can similarly study measurable sets in any Polish space XX, provided that it is equipped with a Borel probability measure μ\mu.22 2 We should point out that the class of measurable sets varies with the choice of the measure μ\mu. For simplicity, we shall assume throughout this article that whenever we speak of measurable sets, it is with respect to some implicitly fixed probability measure. In many applications, sets of measure 00 may be safely ignored, and thus measurability is often a “good enough” substitute for Borelness.

Finally, we also often consider the so-called Baire-measurable sets. The notion of Baire-measurability is analogous to measurability, but it is typically easier to work with. Furthermore, it is defined purely topologically, without reference to a measure or any other additional structure. The role of sets of measure 00 is played by the so-called meager sets, i.e., countable unions of nowhere dense sets. We think of meager sets as “topologically negligible.” A set AA is Baire-measurable if there is a Borel set A′A^{\prime} such that the symmetric difference A​△​A′A\vartriangle A^{\prime} is meager—informally, AA and A′A^{\prime} are “topologically almost equal.” The area studying meager and Baire-measurable sets is called Baire category theory (owing to the older term “sets of first category” for meager sets). For a detailed comparison of measure and Baire category, see the excellent book [Oxt80] by Oxtoby.

1.2.  Borel graphs and their combinatorics

As mentioned earlier, descriptive combinatorics investigates classical combinatorial problems—such as graph coloring, matching, etc.—from the perspective of descriptive set theory. The central notion here is that of a Borel graph:

Definition 1.4 (Borel graphs).

A Borel graph is a graph GG whose vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) is a Polish space and whose edge set E⁡(G)E(G) is a Borel subset of V⁡(G)×V⁡(G)V(G)\times V(G).

In this section, we describe some examples of Borel graphs and highlight a few of their properties that are of interest in descriptive combinatorics.

1.2.1.  The hypercube

For our first example, let ℍ\mathbb{H} be the graph with vertex set {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} in which two bit strings x=(x0,x1,x2,…)x=(x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots), y=(y0,y1,y2,…)∈{0,1}ℕy=(y_{0},y_{1},y_{2},\ldots)\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} are adjacent if and only if they differ in exactly one coordinate, i.e., if there is a unique index n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} such that xn≠ynx_{n}\neq y_{n}. We call ℍ\mathbb{H} the infinite-dimensional hypercube (it can be viewed as the inverse limit of finite-dimensional hypercubes, the first few of which are shown in Fig. 2). The graph ℍ\mathbb{H} is Borel, since it is easy to construct a countable Boolean circuit which, given two infinite bit strings xx and yy, determines if they are adjacent in ℍ\mathbb{H}.

Note that the vertex set of ℍ\mathbb{H} has cardinality 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}. This is typical for graphs studied in descriptive combinatorics, since their vertex sets usually are uncountable Polish spaces.

Next, we observe that, somewhat surprisingly and in contrast to finite-dimensional Boolean cubes, the graph ℍ\mathbb{H} is disconnected. To see this, recall that the connected component of a vertex xx in a graph GG is the smallest set [x]G⊆V⁡(G)[x]_{G}\subseteq V(G) that contains xx and such that there are no edges joining [x]G[x]_{G} to V⁡(G)∖[x]GV(G)\setminus[x]_{G}. Equivalently, [x]G[x]_{G} is the set of all vertices reachable from xx in GG by a finite path. A graph is connected if it has a single connected component. Now take any vertex x∈{0,1}ℕx\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} in ℍ\mathbb{H}. A moment’s thought reveals that the connected component [x]ℍ[x]_{\mathbb{H}} is the set of all sequences y∈{0,1}ℕy\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} that differ from xx in only finitely many coordinates. For instance, if x=(0,0,0,…)x=(0,0,0,\ldots), then [x]ℍ[x]_{\mathbb{H}} is the set of all bit strings with finitely many 11s. It follows that every connected component of ℍ\mathbb{H} is countable, which implies that ℍ\mathbb{H} has 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}-many components. This is also a typical feature of graphs studied in descriptive combinatorics.

One of the most important parameters studied in graph theory is the chromatic number of a graph:

Definition 1.5 (Independent sets and chromatic numbers).

Let GG be a graph. A subset I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) is GG-independent if no edge of GG joins two vertices in II. The chromatic number χ⁡(G)\chi(G) of GG is the smallest cardinal κ\kappa such that V⁡(G)V(G) can be partitioned into κ\kappa-many GG-independent sets.

Let us compute the chromatic number of ℍ\mathbb{H}:

Proposition 1.6.

We have χ⁡(ℍ)=2\chi(\mathbb{H})=2.

Proof.

Clearly, χ⁡(ℍ)⩾2\chi(\mathbb{H})\geqslant 2. To prove that χ⁡(ℍ)⩽2\chi(\mathbb{H})\leqslant 2, we need to partition {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} into two ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent sets. To this end, choose an arbitrary representative from every connected component of ℍ\mathbb{H}. For x∈{0,1}ℕx\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, let rep⁡(x)\mathrm{rep}(x) be the representative from [x]ℍ[x]_{\mathbb{H}}. Since xx and rep⁡(x)\mathrm{rep}(x) belong to the same component of ℍ\mathbb{H}, they differ in finitely many coordinates. Thus, we can let δ⁡(x)\delta(x) be the number of coordinates where xx and rep⁡(x)\mathrm{rep}(x) differ and define

A\displaystyle A\, ≔{x∈{0,1}ℕ:δ⁡(x) is even},\displaystyle\coloneqq\,\{x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,\text{$\delta(x)$ is even}\},
B\displaystyle B\, ≔{x∈{0,1}ℕ:δ⁡(x) is odd}.\displaystyle\coloneqq\,\{x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,\text{$\delta(x)$ is odd}\}.

If xx and yy are neighbors in ℍ\mathbb{H}, then rep⁡(x)=rep⁡(y)\mathrm{rep}(x)=\mathrm{rep}(y), and hence |δ⁡(x)−δ⁡(y)|=1|\delta(x)-\delta(y)|=1. Therefore, the sets AA and BB are ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent and partition {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, as desired. ∎

Since we know that χ⁡(ℍ)=2\chi(\mathbb{H})=2, it makes sense to ask the following question:

Can the set {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} be partitioned into two Borel ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent sets?

This is a special case of the following general problem:

Definition 1.7 (Borel chromatic numbers).

Let GG be a Borel graph. The Borel chromatic number χ𝖡​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G) of GG is the smallest κ∈{0,1,2,…,ℵ0,2ℵ0}\kappa\in\{0,1,2,\ldots,\aleph_{0},2^{\aleph_{0}}\} such that V⁡(G)V(G) can be partitioned into κ\kappa-many Borel GG-independent sets.33 3 Note that, by definition, if χ𝖡​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G) is uncountable, then χ𝖡​(G)=2ℵ0\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)=2^{\aleph_{0}}. This convention is motivated by the fact that every uncountable Polish space has cardinality 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}. However, it may still be meaningful to ask whether V⁡(G)V(G) can be partitioned into κ\kappa-many Borel GG-independent sets for some ℵ0<κ<2ℵ0\aleph_{0}<\kappa<2^{\aleph_{0}}; see [Ges11] for further discussion. This issue will not play a major role in this article, since we shall be mostly interested in the case when χ𝖡​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G) is finite. The measurable and Baire-measurable chromatic numbers χ𝖬​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(G) and χ𝖡𝖬​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{BM}}(G) are defined analogously.

It turns out that, although the chromatic number of ℍ\mathbb{H} is 22, its Borel chromatic number is uncountable!

Proposition 1.8 ([KM20, §4.3]).

The set {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} cannot be partitioned into countably many Borel ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent sets. In other words, χ𝖡​(ℍ)=2ℵ0\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(\mathbb{H})=2^{\aleph_{0}}.

Actually, we even have χ𝖬​(ℍ)=χ𝖡𝖬​(ℍ)=2ℵ0\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(\mathbb{H})=\chi_{\mathsf{BM}}(\mathbb{H})=2^{\aleph_{0}} (and, of course, both χ𝖬​(ℍ)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(\mathbb{H}) and χ𝖡𝖬​(ℍ)\chi_{\mathsf{BM}}(\mathbb{H}) are lower bounds for χ𝖡​(ℍ)\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(\mathbb{H})). To prove this, one shows that every measurable ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent set must have measure 00, while every Baire-measurable ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent set must be meager. Since countable unions of measure-00 or meager sets are still measure-00 or meager respectively, it is impossible to cover the entire space {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} by countably many measurable or Baire-measurable ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent sets.

One interpretation of Proposition 1.8 is that there is no “explicit” partition of the vertex set of ℍ\mathbb{H} into two—or even countably many—ℍ\mathbb{H}-independent sets. What makes the construction in the proof of Proposition 1.6 “inexplicit” is the very first step, namely choosing a single vertex in each connected component of ℍ\mathbb{H}. This step implicitly invokes the so-called Axiom of Choice:

Axiom 1.9 (Choice).

If ℱ\mathcal{F} is a family of nonempty sets, then there is a way to pick one element from each set in ℱ\mathcal{F}. Formally, there is a function 𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐢𝐜𝐞\mathbf{choice} that assigns to each A∈ℱA\in\mathcal{F} an element 𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐢𝐜𝐞⁡(A)∈A\mathbf{choice}(A)\in A.

The Axiom of Choice is part of the axiom system ZFC (Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the Axiom of Choice) and plays a crucial role in the foundations of mathematics. While most other axioms of ZFC assert the existence of concrete sets, such as the powerset 𝒫⁡(A)\mathcal{P}(A) of a given set AA, the Axiom of Choice postulates the existence of a choice function without actually describing how the choice is to be made. In this sense, the Axiom of Choice is non-constructive—so much so that in the past it was viewed with deep suspicion by many mathematicians. After all, how can we assert that something exists without being able to provide even a single example? Although by now the controversy around the Axiom of Choice has largely died down and most mathematicians use it without reservation, it is still true that the Axiom of Choice—and hence our proof of Proposition 1.6 based on it—is inherently non-constructive. From this perspective, Proposition 1.8 says that it is impossible to come up with an alternative, constructive argument---at least if by ‘‘constructive’’ we mean ‘‘Borel.’’44 4 This is not the only way in which the Axiom of Choice affects chromatic numbers of graphs. For instance, the following remarkable fact was established by Galvin and Komjáth [GK91]: the statement that the chromatic number is well-defined for every graph GG is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice.

1.2.2.  Translation and rotation

In the remainder of this article we shall be concerned with Borel graphs GG of bounded degree, meaning that there is a natural number d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} such that every vertex of GG has at most dd neighbors. A typical example is the graph GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} with vertex set ℝ\mathbb{R} in which vertices xx and yy are adjacent if and only if |x−y|=1|x-y|=1. In other words, each x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} has precisely two neighbors in GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}}: x−1x-1 and x+1x+1. It follows that every connected component of GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} is a bi-infinite path (i.e., a path infinite in both directions). In particular, just like the hypercube graph ℍ\mathbb{H} from §1.2.1, GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} has 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}-many countable connected components. (This fact can also be observed directly, since the vertices in the half-open interval [0,1)[0,1) belong to distinct components.) Clearly, χ⁡(Gtr)=2\chi(G_{\mathrm{tr}})=2. In contrast to the graph ℍ\mathbb{H} from §1.2.1 however, we can explicitly describe a partition of GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} into two independent sets AA and BB: for every integer n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, put the points in the interval [n,n+1)[n,n+1) in AA if nn is even and in BB if nn is odd (see Fig. 3). This yields

A=⋃k∈ℤ[2k,2k+1)andB=⋃k∈ℤ[2k−1,2k).A\,=\,\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}[2k,2k+1)\quad\text{and}\quad B\,=\,\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}[2k-1,2k).

These sets are Borel, so we in fact have χ𝖡​(Gtr)=2\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G_{\mathrm{tr}})=2.

Next we fix a number α∈(0,1)∖ℚ\alpha\in(0,1)\setminus\mathbb{Q} and define a graph GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} as follows. The vertex set of GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} is the half-open unit interval [0,1)[0,1). Two vertices xx, y∈[0,1)y\in[0,1) are adjacent in GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} if and only if y−x=±α(mod1)y-x=\pm\alpha\pmod{1}. Again, every vertex xx has precisely two neighbors, namely x+α(mod1)x+\alpha\pmod{1} and x−α(mod1)x-\alpha\pmod{1}. (Another way of thinking about this graph is by “wrapping” the unit interval around a circle, which turns adding α\alpha modulo 11 into rotation by the angle 2​π​α2\pi\alpha.) Since α\alpha is irrational, it is not hard to see that GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} has 2ℵ02^{\aleph_{0}}-many connected components, each of which is a bi-infinite path. In other words, the graphs GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} and GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} are isomorphic. In particular, χ⁡(Grot)=2\chi(G_{\mathrm{rot}})=2. But can we describe a bipartition of GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} explicitly? An attempt to adapt the construction used for GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} fails, although it does yield a partition of GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} into three Borel independent sets (see Fig. 4). In fact, it turns out that no explicit bipartition of GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} exists. This statement is made precise by the following proposition:

Proposition 1.10 ([CMT16, 2]).

We have χ𝖡​(Grot)=3\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G_{\mathrm{rot}})=3. Furthermore, χ𝖬​(Grot)=χ𝖡𝖬​(Grot)=3\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(G_{\mathrm{rot}})=\chi_{\mathsf{BM}}(G_{\mathrm{rot}})=3 as well.

In other words, GtrG_{\mathrm{tr}} and GrotG_{\mathrm{rot}} are two graphs that are combinatorially isomorphic, but the topological structures on their vertex sets affect their Borel, measurable, and Baire-measurable chromatic numbers in different ways.

1.2.3.  Locally checkable labeling problems

In the above examples, we have been interested in chromatic numbers of graphs as well as in their Borel, measurable, etc. analogs. Naturally, there are many other combinatorial concepts we may want to study. Many of them fall into the general framework of locally checkable labelling (LCL) problems (also known as local coloring problems). In an LCL problem Π\Pi, we are asked to assign labels from a finite set Λ\Lambda to the vertices of a graph GG in such a way that certain constraints are satisfied. The constraints must be “local” in the sense that they can be checked by looking at the labels of each vertex and its neighbors. For a formal (and somewhat more general) definition, see, e.g., [Ber20, §2.A.1]. For our purposes, it will suffice to give a few examples that illustrate what sort of problems fall into this category.

The prototypical example is the kk-coloring problem: assign the labels Λ={1,…,k}\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,k\}, referred to as “colors,” to the vertices of GG so that the label of each vertex is distinct from the labels of its neighbors. Note that this is a “local” constraint in the sense described above: it only involves comparing the label of a vertex to those of its neighbors. By definition, the set of all vertices receiving a particular label in a kk-coloring must be a GG-independent set, and hence GG admits a kk-coloring if and only if χ⁡(G)⩽k\chi(G)\leqslant k.

Another well-studied problem is the Maximal Independent Set (MIS) problem: find an independent set I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) that is maximal under inclusion. This can be interpreted as an LCL problem as follows. We can encode a set I⊆V⁡(G)I\subseteq V(G) by its characteristic function, which assigns the labels Λ={0,1}\Lambda=\{0,1\} to the vertices of GG. It is easy to see that II is an MIS if and only if this labelling satisfies the following “local” constraint:

If a vertex is labeled 11, then all its neighbors are labeled 00, while if a vertex is labeled 00, then at least one of its neighbors is labeled 11.

As our last example, consider the perfect matching problem: find a set of edges M⊆E⁡(G)M\subseteq E(G) such that every vertex is incident to exactly one edge in MM. If x​yxy is an edge in MM, then we say that the vertices xx and yy are matched to each other. Thus, a perfect matching splits V⁡(G)V(G) into pairs of matched vertices. To place the perfect matching problem into the LCL framework, let us assume that GG is a graph of bounded degree; more precisely, suppose that every vertex of GG has at most dd neighbors, for some d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}. For each x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), we fix an arbitrary ordering of the neighbors of xx. (If GG is a Borel graph, it is possible to fix such an ordering “in a Borel way,” in the sense that for each ii, the set {(x,y)∈V⁡(G)×V⁡(G):y is the i-th neighbor of x}\{(x,y)\in V(G)\times V(G)\,:\,\text{$y$ is the $i$-th neighbor of $x$}\} is Borel.) Then we can identify a perfect matching with a labeling of V⁡(G)V(G) using the labels Λ={1,…,d}\Lambda=\{1,\ldots,d\} such that a vertex is given the label ii when it is matched to its ii-th neighbor. Such labeling encodes a perfect matching if and only if the following constraint holds:

Let xx be a vertex labeled ii and let yy be the ii-th neighbor of xx. If yy’s label is jj, then xx is the jj-th neighbor of yy.

In other words, if xx is matched to yy, then yy must be matched to xx. This constraint is again “local,” which makes the perfect matching problem an LCL problem (at least on bounded degree graphs).

In descriptive combinatorics, we are interested in Borel solutions to LCL problems:

Definition 1.11 (Borel solutions to LCL problems).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem with label set Λ\Lambda and let GG be a Borel graph. A labeling of the vertices of GG by the labels from Λ\Lambda is a Borel solution to Π\Pi if it fulfills all the constraints of the problem Π\Pi and, additionally, for each label λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, the set of all vertices labeled λ\lambda is Borel.

Measurable and Baire-measurable solutions to Π\Pi are defined analogously.

By applying Definition 1.11 to specific LCL problems, we obtain, as special cases, Borel kk-colorings, Borel maximal independent sets, and Borel perfect matchings. In general, a lot of research in descriptive combinatorics can be seen as addressing the following comprehensive question:

Problem 1.12 (Descriptive complexity of LCL problems).

Given a class 𝒢\mathcal{G} of Borel graphs, which LCL problems admit Borel/measurable/etc. solutions on the graphs in 𝒢\mathcal{G}?

As stated, this question may seem way too general to say anything meaningful about. However, rather surprisingly, some recent work has led to significant progress toward a complete answer! The key to this new work is the discovery of an intimate connection between the answer to Question 1.12 and the complexity of solving the given LCL problem on finite graphs using a distributed algorithm. The second part of this paper is dedicated to a survey of this connection.

2.  Connections to distributed computing

2.1.  The 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model of distributed computation

The area of distributed computing studies computational processes performed by decentralized groups of independent agents. There are several different models of distributed computation that emphasize various aspects of it, such as fault-tolerance, communication bandwidth, etc. For our purposes, the relevant model is called 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} and was formally introduced by Linial in 1992 [Lin92] (although some related results had already been established somewhat earlier, e.g., by Alon, Babai, and Itai [ABI86], Luby [Lub86], and Goldberg, Plotkin, and Shannon [GPS88]). For a comprehensive introduction to this model, see the book [BE13] by Barenboim and Elkin. We now briefly describe the key elements of this model.

The 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model operates on an nn-vertex graph GG. (Note that, in contrast to the examples discussed in §1.2, the graph GG here is finite.) We think of GG as representing a decentralized communication network where each vertex plays the role of a processor and edges represent communication links. The computation proceeds in rounds. During each round, the vertices first perform some local computations and then synchronously broadcast messages to all their neighbors. After a number of rounds, every vertex must generate its own part of the output of the algorithm. For example, if the goal of the algorithm is to solve some LCL problem, then each vertex must eventually decide on its own label. The efficiency of such an algorithm is measured by the number of communication rounds required to produce the output. In particular, there are no restrictions on the complexity of the local computations that the vertices perform during each round (we imagine that the computational resources available to the vertices are infinite) or on the length of the messages that the vertices send to each other.

An important feature of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model is that every vertex of GG is executing the same algorithm. Therefore, to make this model nontrivial, there must be a way to distinguish the vertices from each other. There are two standard symmetry-breaking approaches, leading to the distinction between deterministic and randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms:

  • —

    In the deterministic version of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, each vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) is assigned, as part of its input, an identifier Id⁡(x)\mathrm{Id}(x), which is a string of Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n) bits. It is guaranteed that the identifiers assigned to different vertices are distinct. Subject to this guarantee, the algorithm must always output a correct solution to the problem, regardless of the specific assignment of the identifiers.

  • —

    In the randomized version of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, each vertex may generate an arbitrarily long finite sequence of independent uniformly distributed random bits. The algorithm may fail to produce a correct solution to the problem, but the probability of failure must not exceed 1/n1/n.

We remark that the randomized version of the model is more computationally powerful than the deterministic one. This is because a deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm can be simulated by a randomized one: each vertex can simply generate a random sequence of ⌈3​log2​n⌉\lceil 3\log_{2}n\rceil bits and use it as its identifier—the probability that two identifiers generated in this way coincide is easily seen to be less than 1/n1/n.

If xx and yy are two vertices whose graph distance in GG (i.e., the length of the shortest x​yxy-path) is TT, then no information from yy can reach xx in fewer than TT communication rounds (this explains the name “𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL}” given to the model). Conversely, in TT rounds every vertex can collect all the data present at the vertices at distance at most TT from it. Thus, a TT-round 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm may be construed simply as a function that, given the structure of the radius-TT ball around xx (including all the additional information, such as the assignment of the identifiers or random bit sequences to its vertices), decides on xx’s output. In other words, the complexity of a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm measures how far in the graph an individual vertex should be allowed to “see” in order to be able to produce its own output. Naturally, if every vertex is allowed to “see” the entire graph, then the model trivializes. Thus, we are interested in algorithms that only allow each vertex to access a relatively small part of the graph.

As an illustration, let us consider a simple example. Suppose that GG is an nn-vertex path. Of course, χ⁡(G)=2\chi(G)=2. How fast can a 22-coloring of GG be computed by a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm? Obviously, O⁡(n)O(n) rounds suffice (because in that many rounds each vertex will have access to the entire graph). On the other hand, it is fairly easy to show that o⁡(n)o(n) rounds are not enough:

Proposition 2.1.

There is no o⁡(n)o(n)-round 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm (either deterministic or randomized) that finds a 22-coloring of an nn-vertex path.

Proof.

We give an argument in the deterministic case (leaving the randomized case as a nice exercise to the reader). Suppose that there is a TT-round deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} for 22-coloring an nn-vertex path, where T≪nT\ll n. We can pick three vertices xx, yy, zz such that the distance between xx and yy is even, while the distance between xx and zz is odd, and, furthermore, all the pairwise distances between xx, yy, and zz exceed 2​T2T (see Fig. 5). Fix any assignment of identifiers and let c⁡(x)c(x), c⁡(y)c(y), c⁡(z)c(z) be the colors given by the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} to xx, yy, and zz respectively. In a 22-coloring of a path, the two colors alternate, so we must have c⁡(x)=c⁡(y)≠c⁡(z)c(x)=c(y)\neq c(z). Without loss of generality, say c⁡(x)=c⁡(y)=1c(x)=c(y)=1 and c⁡(z)=2c(z)=2. Now let us exchange the assignments of the identifiers in the interval of length 2​T2T centered around yy with those in the interval centered around zz and let c′​(x)c^{\prime}(x), c′​(y)c^{\prime}(y), c′​(z)c^{\prime}(z) be the colors given to xx, yy, and zz by the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with this new assignment of identifiers. Since the output of 𝒜\mathcal{A} at a vertex is determined by the identifiers in the interval of length 2​T2T centered around it, we have c′​(x)=c′​(z)=1c^{\prime}(x)=c^{\prime}(z)=1 and c′​(y)=2c^{\prime}(y)=2. This is a contradiction since the colors of xx and yy must be the same, while the colors of xx and zz must be different. ∎

2.2.  A sample of results

The first hint of the connection between distributed algorithms and descriptive combinatorics can be obtained by comparing some known results in the two areas. For example, consider the following problem:

Fix a natural number d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}. What is the minimum k=k⁡(d)k=k(d) such that a kk-coloring of a graph of maximum degree dd can be found efficiently?

Here the maximum degree of a graph is the maximum number of neighbors of a vertex. If we interpret the word “efficiently” to mean “with a fast 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm,” then we have the following result:

Theorem 2.2 (Goldberg–Plotkin–Shannon [BE13, §3]).

There exists a deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that finds a (d+1)(d+1)-coloring of an nn-vertex graph of maximum degree dd in O⁡(log∗⁡n)O(\log^{\ast}n) rounds.55 5 Here and in the sequel we treat dd as a constant, meaning that the implied factors in the O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) notation may depend on dd.

In the statement of Theorem 2.2, log∗⁡n\log^{\ast}n is the iterated logarithm of nn, i.e., the number of times the logarithm function must be iteratively applied to nn before the result becomes at most 11. This is an extremely slow growing function. In particular—and most importantly for us—it is asymptotically of order o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n). In a graph of maximum degree dd, a vertex can “see” at most dTd^{T} other vertices in TT rounds of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model. Therefore, if T=o⁡(log⁡n)T=o(\log n), a vertex will definitely not have access to the entire graph. In this sense, o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) rounds is a natural threshold for “truly local” algorithms.

Can we reduce the number of colors to dd? An obvious obstacle is that GG may contain a clique on d+1d+1 vertices, all of which would have to receive different colors. On the other hand, the so-called Brooks’s theorem in graph theory asserts that if d⩾3d\geqslant 3 and GG is a graph of maximum degree dd without a (d+1)(d+1)-clique, then χ⁡(G)⩽d\chi(G)\leqslant d, i.e., a dd-coloring of GG exists [Die17, Theorem 5.2.4]. Nevertheless, it turns out that no efficient deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm can find such a coloring, even if GG has no cycles:

Theorem 2.3 (Chang–Kopelowitz–Pettie [CKP19]).

There is no deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that finds a dd-coloring of an nn-vertex acyclic graph of maximum degree dd in o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) rounds.

In contrast to Theorem 2.3, it is possible to reduce the number of colors using a randomized algorithm:

Theorem 2.4 (Ghaffari–Hirvonen–Kuhn–Maus [Gha+18]).

There exists a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that finds a dd-coloring of an nn-vertex graph GG of maximum degree dd in O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)2)O((\log\log n)^{2}) rounds, provided that d⩾3d\geqslant 3 and GG has no (d+1)(d+1)-cliques.

Now let us turn to the descriptive combinatorics side of the picture. How many colors do we need for a Borel coloring of a Borel graph of maximum degree dd? The first result parallels Theorem 2.2:

Theorem 2.5 (Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic [KST99]).

If GG is a Borel graph of maximum degree dd, then χ𝖡​(G)⩽d+1\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)\leqslant d+1.

On the other hand, reducing the number of colors to dd is impossible even for graphs with no cycles:

Theorem 2.6 (Marks [Mar16]).

For any d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}, there is an acyclic Borel graph GG of maximum degree dd such that χ𝖡​(G)>d\chi_{\mathsf{B}}(G)>d.

However, if we only want a measurable or Baire-measurable coloring, then dd colors suffice:

Theorem 2.7 (Conley–Marks–Tucker-Drob [CMT16]).

If GG is a Borel graph of maximum degree dd, then both χ𝖬​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{M}}(G) and χ𝖡𝖬​(G)\chi_{\mathsf{BM}}(G) are at most dd, provided that d⩾3d\geqslant 3 and GG has no (d+1)(d+1)-cliques.

Theorems 2.2–2.4 and 2.5–2.7 clearly mirror each other. It seems that deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms somehow correspond to Borel constructions, while randomized algorithms—to measurable and Baire-measurable ones. It turns out that, indeed, this is not a coincidence and one can prove some general connections of this form.

2.3.  Efficient distributed algorithms yield descriptive results

In [Ber20], the following general result is established:

Theorem 2.8 (Bernshteyn [Ber20]).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a class of finite graphs closed under adding isolated vertices and let GG be a Borel graph of bounded degree all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Fix an LCL problem Π\Pi.

  1. (a)

    If Π\Pi can be solved on nn-vertex graphs from 𝒢\mathcal{G} by an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm, then GG admits a Borel solution to Π\Pi.

  2. (b)

    If Π\Pi can be solved on nn-vertex graphs from 𝒢\mathcal{G} by an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm, then GG admits both a measurable and a Baire-measurable solution to Π\Pi.

In short, efficient deterministic algorithms yield Borel solutions, while efficient randomized algorithms yield measurable and Baire-measurable solutions. The following implications are special cases of Theorem 2.8:

Theorem 2.2 ⟹Theorem 2.5,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ \text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:KST}},
Theorem 2.4 ⟹Theorem 2.7,\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ \text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:yesdmeas}},
Theorem 2.6 ⟹Theorem 2.3.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ \text{Theorem\penalty\ \ref{theo:nod}}.

In addition to its theoretical significance, Theorem 2.8 has a number of applications to specific problems. For instance, if we already know an efficient 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for some LCL problem, we can then use it to derive corresponding results in descriptive combinatorics. Several instances of this are given in [Ber20]. For example, Theorem 2.8, together with known distributed algorithms due to Chung, Pettie, and Su [CPS17], is used in [Ber20, §3.B] to obtain asymptotically optimal upper bounds on the measurable chromatic number of Borel graphs without short cycles. In the opposite direction, impossibility results in descriptive combinatorics yield lower bounds on the running time of distributed algorithms. In a recent paper [Bra+21], Brandt et al. used this idea to derive new lower bounds for distributed algorithms via a version of the so-called determinacy method that was originally developed by Marks to prove Theorem 2.6.

Let us now say a few words about the proof of Theorem 2.8. The proof of part (a) is actually not too difficult:

Proof of Theorem 2.8(a) (sketch).

Suppose that Π\Pi is solved on nn-vertex graphs from 𝒢\mathcal{G} by an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The idea is to simulate the execution of the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} on the given Borel graph GG by “pretending” that GG is finite.

Let dd be the maximum degree of GG (which is finite by assumption). Take a very large natural number nn and let T≪log⁡nT\ll\log n be the running time of 𝒜\mathcal{A} on nn-vertex graphs. Let SS be the set of all bit strings of length ⌈log2⁡n⌉\lceil\log_{2}n\rceil.

Claim 0.

There is a Borel labeling Id:V⁡(G)→S\mathrm{Id}\colon V(G)\to S such that Id⁡(x)≠Id⁡(y)\mathrm{Id}(x)\neq\mathrm{Id}(y) whenever x≠yx\neq y and the graph distance between xx and yy is at most 2​T+22T+2.

Proof of the claim.

Define an auxiliary graph G′G^{\prime} with the same vertex set as GG where distinct vertices xx and yy are adjacent if and only if their graph distance in GG is at most 2​T+22T+2. It is not hard to see that the graph G′G^{\prime} is Borel. Since |S|⩾n|S|\geqslant n, we just need to find a Borel nn-coloring of G′G^{\prime}. The maximum degree of G′G^{\prime} is at most d2​T+2d^{2T+2}, which is less than nn since 2​T+2≪log⁡n2T+2\ll\log n. Therefore, by Theorem 2.5, G′G^{\prime} has a Borel nn-coloring, as desired. ∎

We treat the bit string Id⁡(x)\mathrm{Id}(x) as a substitute for an identifier of xx. By construction, although there may be other vertices with the same identifier, they are far from xx in GG. In particular, if xx explores its radius-TT ball in GG, it will only see distinct identifiers. Since the algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} applied on nn-vertex graphs doesn’t allow a vertex to see outside its radius-TT ball, we many run 𝒜\mathcal{A} on GG for TT rounds (as if GG had nn vertices) using the function Id\mathrm{Id} in place of the identifier assignment. The output labeling will then be a solution to Π\Pi, and, since Id\mathrm{Id} is a Borel assignment, one can show that the output will also be Borel. ∎

Arguments similar to the above proof sketch are common in distributed computing theory. For example, an analogous approach was used by Chang, Kopelowitz, and Pettie in [CKP19] to prove that no LCL problem can have deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity in the interval between ω⁡(log∗⁡n)\omega(\log^{\ast}n) and o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n).

The proof of Theorem 2.8(b) is quite a bit more involved, and we won’t venture to explain it here. Let us just mention one interesting feature of it. The key tool used to prove Theorem 2.8(b) is the measurable version of the Local Lemma, which is also established in [Ber20]. The Local Lemma is a well-known powerful tool in probabilistic combinatorics that is often used to show that a given LCL problem has a solution. The measurable version of this lemma additionally guarantees that the solution is measurable. And here we encounter another point of interaction between descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing: the proof of the measurable Local Lemma in [Ber20] crucially relies on the efficient randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for the Local Lemma developed by Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17].

2.4.  Perfect harmony between the two worlds: continuous solutions

Theorem 2.8 allows one to turn efficient distributed algorithms into results in descriptive combinatorics. It is natural to ask if some sort of converse to Theorem 2.8 also holds, i.e., if we can obtain efficient algorithms from descriptive results. While in general this question remains widely open, there is one salient case in which an exact correspondence between the descriptive and the distributed worlds has been established. This case concerns continuous solutions to LCL problems.

Definition 2.9 (Continuous solutions to LCL problems).

Let Π\Pi be an LCL problem with label set Λ\Lambda and let GG be a Borel graph. A labeling of the vertices of GG by the labels from Λ\Lambda is a continuous solution to Π\Pi if it fulfills all the constraints of the problem Π\Pi and, additionally, for each label λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda, the set of all vertices labeled λ\lambda is open.

Note that the set of all vertices receiving a given label in a continuous solution must be both open and closed—clopen, in short. Hence, it is only interesting to study continuous solutions to LCL problems on graphs GG such that the space V⁡(G)V(G) has many clopen subsets. Specifically, we focus on zero-dimensional spaces, i.e., spaces whose topology is generated by clopen sets. Even though familiar spaces such as ℝ\mathbb{R} do not have any nontrivial clopen sets, zero-dimensional spaces are rather common. For example, the space {0,1}ℕ\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} is zero-dimensional. Another example of a zero-dimensional Polish space is ℝ∖ℚ\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}. Also, given any Polish space XX, it is possible to refine the topology on XX to make it zero-dimensional without changing the Borel sets [Kec95, §13].

The main result we want to describe in this section says, roughly, that an LCL problem can be solved continuously if and only if it can be solved via an efficient deterministic distributed algorithm. To make this statement precise, we need to specify a particular graph or a class of graphs on which we attempt to solve the problem. While it is possible to make the statement somewhat more general, it will be convenient to consider classes of graphs that look very symmetric, such as regular trees or multi-dimensional grids. The following general definition includes these examples as special cases:

Definition 2.10 (Γ\Gamma-graphs).

Let Γ\Gamma be a group generated by a fixed finite symmetric66 6 A subset S⊆ΓS\subseteq\Gamma is symmetric if for all γ∈S\gamma\in S, γ−1∈S\gamma^{-1}\in S as well. set S⊆ΓS\subseteq\Gamma.

The Cayley graph Cay⁡(Γ)\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma) of Γ\Gamma corresponding to SS is the graph with vertex set Γ\Gamma that includes, for every γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma and σ∈S\sigma\in S, an edge from γ\gamma to σ​γ\sigma\gamma. To be precise, we view Cay⁡(Γ)\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma) as an edge-labeled graph, where the label of the edge (γ,σ​γ)(\gamma,\sigma\gamma) is σ\sigma, but the reader may safely ignore this technicality.

A Γ\Gamma-graph is a graph (with edge labels) in which every connected component is isomorphic to Cay⁡(Γ)\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma).

For instance, the Cayley graph of the additive group ℤ\mathbb{Z} with generating set S={1,−1}S=\{1,-1\} is a bi-infinite path. Similarly, the Cayley graph of ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d} with respect to an appropriately chosen generating set is an infinite dd-dimensional square grid. On the other hand, the Cayley graph of the free group 𝔽d\mathbb{F}_{d} of rank dd is an infinite dd-regular tree.

Given any group Γ\Gamma with a finite symmetric generating set SS, there is a canonical way to define a particular Γ\Gamma-graph 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} on a zero-dimensional vertex set, called the shift graph of Γ\Gamma. The shift graph 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} is an extremely important example that occupies a central place not only in descriptive combinatorics, but also in such areas as ergodic theory and topological dynamics. Before giving the general definition, it will be instructive to consider the special case Γ=ℤ\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}, with generating set S={1,−1}S=\{1,-1\}. For a subset A⊆ℤA\subseteq\mathbb{Z} and an element n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, we write

A+n≔{m+n:m∈A}.A+n\,\coloneqq\,\{m+n\,:\,m\in A\}.

The set A+nA+n can naturally be seen as a “shift” of AA by nn (hence the term “shift graph”). We say that a set A⊆ℤA\subseteq\mathbb{Z} is aperiodic if A+n≠AA+n\neq A for every non-zero n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}. This is equivalent to saying that the characteristic function 𝟏A\mathbf{1}_{A} of AA is not periodic, i.e., there is no integer n≠0n\neq 0 such that 𝟏A​(m)=𝟏A​(m+n)\mathbf{1}_{A}(m)=\mathbf{1}_{A}(m+n) for all m∈ℤm\in\mathbb{Z}. The shift graph 𝐒ℤ\mathbf{S}_{\mathbb{Z}} is the graph whose vertices are the aperiodic subsets of ℤ\mathbb{Z} and in which every aperiodic set AA has two neighbors: A+1A+1 and A−1A-1. Thus, the connected component of AA in 𝐒ℤ\mathbf{S}_{\mathbb{Z}} is the following infinite path:

⋯—(A−2)—(A−1)—(A)—(A+1)—(A+2)—⋯\cdots\ \text{\textemdash}\ (A-2)\ \text{\textemdash}\ (A-1)\ \text{\textemdash}\ (A)\ \text{\textemdash}\ (A+1)\ \text{\textemdash}\ (A+2)\ \text{\textemdash}\ \cdots

(Since AA is aperiodic, all the vertices on this path are distinct.) In particular, every component of 𝐒ℤ\mathbf{S}_{\mathbb{Z}} is isomorphic to the Cayley graph of ℤ\mathbb{Z}, so it is indeed a ℤ\mathbb{Z}-graph.

Now for the general construction. Let Γ\Gamma be a group with a finite symmetric generating set SS. For a set A⊆ΓA\subseteq\Gamma and an element γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma, let

γ​A≔{γ​α:α∈A}.\gamma A\,\coloneqq\,\{\gamma\alpha\,:\,\alpha\in A\}.

A subset A⊆ΓA\subseteq\Gamma is aperiodic if γ​A≠A\gamma A\neq A for all non-identity elements γ∈Γ\gamma\in\Gamma. The vertices of 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} are the aperiodic subsets A⊆ΓA\subseteq\Gamma, and for every A∈V⁡(𝐒Γ)A\in V(\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma}) and σ∈S\sigma\in S, 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} includes an edge from AA to σ​A\sigma A labeled σ\sigma. By construction, for each A∈V⁡(𝐒Γ)A\in V(\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma}), the mapping γ↦γ​A\gamma\mapsto\gamma A establishes an isomorphism between Cay⁡(Γ)\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma) and the connected component of AA in 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} (the fact that AA is aperiodic guarantees that this mapping is injective). Thus, 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} is a Γ\Gamma-graph. Furthermore, by identifying each subset of Γ\Gamma with its characteristic function, we can view V⁡(𝐒Γ)V(\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma}) as a subset of {0,1}Γ\{0,1\}^{\Gamma}, which makes 𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} a Borel graph on a zero-dimensional Polish space.

We now have the following result, obtained independently by Bernshteyn [Ber21] and Seward (unpublished):

Theorem 2.11 (Bernshteyn [Ber21]/Seward).

Let Γ\Gamma be a group generated by a finite symmetric set S⊆ΓS\subseteq\Gamma. For every LCL problem Π\Pi, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    𝐒Γ\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma} admits a continuous solution to Π\Pi.

  2. (ii)

    There is an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that solves Π\Pi on nn-vertex subgraphs of the Cayley graph Cay⁡(Γ)\mathrm{Cay}(\Gamma).

The implication (ii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (i) of Theorem 2.11 is proved in a manner analogous to the proof of Theorem 2.8(a) sketched in §2.3. The implication (i) ⟹\Longrightarrow (ii) is significantly more difficult and involves a careful analysis of the structure of continuous functions on V⁡(𝐒Γ)V(\mathbf{S}_{\Gamma}). Interestingly, this analysis again relies, among other things, on tools from computer science such as the so-called method of conditional probabilities. It also builds on earlier work of Gao–Jackson–Seward [GJS16], Seward–Tucker-Drob [ST16], and Elek [Ele18].

Theorem 2.11 explains the analogies between known results in continuous combinatorics and distributed computing. For example, in the case Γ=ℤd\Gamma=\mathbb{Z}^{d}, the continuous combinatorics of the shift graph have been studied in detail by Gao et al. [Gao+18]. Similarly, Brandt et al. [Bra+17] investigated the LCL problems that can be solved on dd-dimensional square grids by efficient distributed algorithms. The results obtained by these two groups of researchers—independently and using different methods—perfectly parallel each other, exactly as Theorem 2.11 predicts.

2.5.  Baire-measurable solutions to LCL problems on trees

The last result we would like to mention is a very recent theorem that establishes a perfect equivalence between yet another pair of facets of the worlds of descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing:

Theorem 2.12 (Brandt et al. [Bra+21]).

Fix d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}. For every LCL problem Π\Pi, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    Every Borel graph GG in which every component is an infinite dd-regular tree admits a Baire-measurable solution to Π\Pi.

  2. (ii)

    There is an O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n)-round deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that solves Π\Pi on nn-vertex trees of maximum degree dd.

This is a truly inspiring result, which highlights how deep the connections between descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing lie. What makes it different from Theorems 2.8 and 2.11 is that the complexity bound on the distributed algorithm here is O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n), not o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n). Note that in O⁡(log⁡n)O(\log n) rounds, a vertex of an nn-vertex tree of maximum degree d⩾3d\geqslant 3 is guaranteed to discover a vertex of degree less than dd—and hence this algorithm cannot be directly used on a dd-regular graph GG. Unsurprisingly, the proof of the implication (ii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (i) in Theorem 2.12 is considerably more difficult than the proof of Theorem 2.8(a). In fact, both implications in Theorem 2.12 are highly nontrivial. The high-level idea of the argument is to isolate a certain combinatorial property of LCL problems and show that this property is equivalent to each of (i), (ii) separately (the former equivalence was established by Bernshteyn (unpublished), the latter—by Brandt et al. [Bra+21]).

2.6.  Final thoughts and open problems

The intimate interactions between descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing have only very recently been discovered, and most questions about them remain open. Perhaps the central open problem is this:

Problem 2.13.

Is there a version of Theorem 2.11 for Borel solutions to LCL problems? In other words, is there a precise algorithmic counterpart to the notion of a Borel solution (similar to how o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms are equivalent to continuous solutions)?

The same questions for measurable and (except for graphs with no cycles) Baire-measurable solutions are also open. Even on graphs as simple as dd-regular trees, many open questions remain. The diagram in Fig. 6 summarizes our knowledge regarding the complexity of LCL problems on dd-regular trees. In particular, we know that there are LCL problems that admit Borel solutions but cannot be solved by an o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n)-round randomized algorithm, but there are also LCL problems that can be solved by such an algorithm but do not admit Borel solutions. Therefore, a new algorithmic framework seems to be needed to capture the notion of a Borel solution precisely.

On classes of graphs other than trees, our knowledge is even scanter. For example, the following basic question is open:

Problem 2.14.

Fix an integer d⩾2d\geqslant 2. Does there exist an LCL problem Π\Pi such that the shift graph 𝐒ℤd\mathbf{S}_{\mathbb{Z}^{d}} admits a measurable solution to Π\Pi but not a Borel one? What about Baire-measurable solutions?

Another area with close ties to distributed computing and descriptive combinatorics is the study of so-called finitary factors of i.i.d. processes. This is a class of particularly well-behaved random processes on networks of great interest in probability theory. Finitary factors of i.i.d. processes can be used to create a complexity hierarchy of LCL problems, and Grebík and Rozhoň recently discovered that in many cases this hierarchy parallels the one arising from considering descriptive and 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity. For more details on this exciting connection, see the papers [GR21] by Grebík and Rozhoň and [Bra+21] by Brandt et al.

In spite of all the open problems mentioned above, it really does appear that the combination of tools from descriptive set theory and distributed computing is the key to attaining a deep understanding of the behavior of LCL problems under various “effectiveness” requirements. Exciting discoveries await, and they will surely enrich descriptive combinatorics and distributed computing alike.
